extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claims recite judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, mental processes, laws of nature/natural phenomena) under the MPEP §2106 subject-matter eligibility framework. Focused on identifying groupings of abstract ideas and how to analyze claims (Step 2A/2B) including special procedures for tentative abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial or Legal Interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Commercial interactions" or "legal interactions" include agreements in the form of contracts, legal obligations, advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors, and business relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that are "squarely about creating a contractual relationship" or otherwise directed to commercial/legal interactions are abstract ideas. Examples and case citations: buySAFE (transaction performance guaranty—contractual relationship); Bancorp (managing stable value protected life insurance policy via calculations); Accenture v. Guidewire (processing insurance claims under an insurance policy); Fort Properties (legal obligation—tax-free exchanges); Bilski (hedging); Alice (mitigating settlement risk/intermediated settlement); In re Comiskey (arbitration); Ultramercial (using advertising as exchange/currency); In re Ferguson (structuring a sales force); In re Maucorps (algorithm for optimal business visits); OIP Techs. v. Amazon (offer-based price optimization); Credit Acceptance (processing credit applications/financing packages); Dealertrack (processing through a clearing-house). Examiner takeaway: identify when the claim's focus is on these business/legal/commercial practices as an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing Personal Behavior or Relationships or Interactions Between People
rubrics_metrics.description: This sub-grouping includes social activities, teaching, and following rules or instructions—i.e., methods of organizing or managing human activity and interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that recite managing personal behavior or social interactions may be abstract ideas. Examples: Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One (storing user-selected pre-set spending limits—budgeting/tracking financial transactions); BASCOM (filtering content); BSG Tech v. Buyseasons (considering historical usage when inputting data); In re Meyer (mental process for neurologist testing); Voter Verified (voting, verifying votes, submitting for tabulation—voting as longstanding human activity); Interval Licensing v. AOL (attention manager providing info without disrupting primary activity); In re Marco Guldenaar (rules for playing games—dice game wagering); In re Brown (assigning hair designs); Bilski (series of instructions how to hedge). Examiner takeaway: compare claimed activity to longstanding human practices for eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental Processes (abstract idea grouping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental processes are concepts that can be performed in the human mind, or by a human using a pen and paper (e.g., observations, evaluations, judgments, opinions) and are treated as abstract ideas by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic rule: methods which can be performed mentally or which are the equivalent of human mental work are unpatentable abstract ideas (citing CyberSource, Benson, Mayo, Flook). Examiners should treat "mental processes" as a type of abstract idea regardless of statutory claim category (product or process). The guidance below (points A–D) explains how to determine if a claim limitation recites a mental process, with numerous case examples. Consider whether limitations are practicable for a human mind, whether physical aids change the analysis, and whether computer implementation changes the characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: A. Claim limitations that cannot practically be performed in the human mind do not recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim contains limitations that the human mind is not equipped to perform practically, it does not recite a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should find these claims outside the mental-process grouping. Case examples: SRI Int’l v. Cisco (network monitors/analyzing network packets—human mind not equipped); SiRF (GPS pseudorange calculations); Synopsys (specific data encryption method requiring several-step data manipulation); Research Corp. Techs. (halftone rendering involving computer data structures). Contrasting examples of claims that do recite mental processes include: Electric Power Group (collecting, analyzing, displaying data at high level of generality), University of Utah Research Foundation v. Ambry (comparing BRCA sequences in any way), Classen (collecting and comparing known info), In re Brown (identifying head shape/applying hair designs). Examiner takeaway: focus on whether the limitation can be practically performed mentally (not merely theoretically).

rubrics_metrics.name: B. Claim limitations that encompass human performance mentally (with or without physical aids) recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim recites a limitation that a human could practically perform mentally, even aided by pen and paper or similar physical aids, the limitation falls within the mental processes grouping and is an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical aids (pen/paper, slide rule) do not negate the mental nature of a limitation; they only account for memory/capacity differences. Examples: Benson (algorithm convertible to mental calculation); CyberSource (constructing a map of credit card numbers could be done by writing down transactions); Synopsys (translating logic description to hardware description could be done mentally/with pencil and paper); Flook (computations by pencil and paper); University of Florida Rsch Found. v. GE (reliance on specification to determine mental performability). Examiner takeaway: consult the specification and claim detail to see if claimed steps are simply mental operations (even with simple physical aids).

rubrics_metrics.name: C. A claim that requires a computer may still recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer implementation does not automatically remove a claim from the mental-process grouping; courts have found computer-implemented steps to still be abstract ideas where the underlying concept can be performed mentally or with pen and paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should carefully review the claim and specification to determine whether the applicant is simply claiming a concept performed: (1) on a generic computer (e.g., Voter Verified, Versata), (2) in a computer environment (e.g., Symantec, FairWarning), or (3) using a computer as a tool to perform the concept (e.g., Mortgage Grader, Berkheimer). Examples and rationale: Benson (mental algorithm within a computer); Mortgage Grader (anonymous loan shopping could be performed by humans); Versata (determining a price using organizational/product hierarchies implemented on general-purpose hardware still directed to abstract idea). Examiner takeaway: determine if claimed computer elements add anything that precludes human performance or are merely generic/directional. If the specification describes the concept as human cognitive actions implemented on a computer, treat as mental process.

rubrics_metrics.name: C.1 Performing a mental process on a generic computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing a mental-process-type concept on a generic computer can still be an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Voter Verified (voting/verifying/submitting—human cognitive actions performed on a computer still abstract); Versata (price determination on general purpose hardware still an abstract idea). Examiner takeaway: implementation on general-purpose computer hardware does not inherently confer eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: C.2 Performing a mental process in a computer environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing a mental-process-type concept within a computer environment can still be an abstract idea if the claim steps are analogous to human cognitive actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Symantec (electronic post office receiving, screening, distributing email analogous to human mail decisions); FairWarning (detecting misuse via rule-based analysis analogous to human fraud detection questions). Examiner takeaway: compare claimed rules/analysis to analogous human questions/actions described in the specification and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: C.3 Using a computer as a tool to perform a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a computer merely as a tool to perform what is otherwise a mental concept renders the claim a mental process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples: Mortgage Grader (grading/comparing loan packages—concept of anonymous loan shopping could be done without a computer); Berkheimer (parsing and comparing data recited at a high level of generality—computer merely used as a tool). Examiner takeaway: determine whether computer implementation is essential or merely a tool for performing an otherwise mental concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: D. Both product and process claims may recite a mental process
rubrics_metrics.description: Both product claims (systems, computer-readable media) and process claims can be directed to mental processes and thus to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of product claims reciting mental processes: Content Extraction (API for extracting/processing info from hard-copy documents), Mortgage Grader (system enabling anonymous loan shopping), CyberSource (computer-readable medium for detecting fraud), Symantec (electronic post office), Voter Verified (self-verifying voting system), Electric Power Group (real-time monitoring system), Versata (computer readable media implementing price determination). Process claim examples discussed in earlier subsections (Flook, Benson, Berkheimer, Synopsys, Ambry Genetics). Examiner takeaway: do not assume product (apparatus/media) claims are immune—analyze claim substance and generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative Abstract Ideas (procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'tentative abstract idea' is a claim limitation that an examiner believes should be treated as an abstract idea even though it does not fall within enumerated groupings (mathematical concepts, methods of organizing human activity, mental processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: evaluate under the subject matter eligibility framework—(1) If the claim as a whole integrates the tentative abstract idea into a practical application, the claim is not directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible (Pathway B). (2) If it does not integrate into a practical application, it is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further analysis at Step 2B; if the claim as a whole provides an inventive concept at Step 2B, it is eligible (Pathway C). (3) If the claim does not provide an inventive concept at Step 2B, bring the application to the attention of the Technology Center (TC) director; a rejection of a claim reciting a tentative abstract idea must be approved by the TC director (approval recorded in the file), and a justification must be provided for treating the limitation as an abstract idea. The TC Director will authorize use of form paragraph 7.05.017 and include signature; public notification may follow. Interview guidance: examiner may conduct interview to advance prosecution; interview with TC Director is not required to withdraw/maintain rejection once TC Director has given initial approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Nature, Natural Phenomena & Products of Nature (judicial exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature and natural phenomena include naturally occurring principles/relations and nature-based products that are naturally occurring or lack markedly different characteristics from what occurs in nature; these are judicial exceptions to patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts describe these as physical phenomena, scientific principles, natural laws, and products of nature. Foundational rationale: basic tools of scientific/technological work are not patentable (Funk Bros., Diamond v. Chakrabarty). Examples listed by courts: (i) isolated DNA (Myriad); (ii) cloned farm animal (In re Roslin); (iii) correlation between non-coding and coding DNA regions (Genetic Techs. v. Merial); (iv) metabolic correlation (Mayo); (v) myeloperoxidase correlation and cardiovascular risk (Cleveland Clinic v. True Health); (vi) electromagnetism to transmit signals (O’Reilly v. Morse); (vii) bacterial qualities (Funk); (viii) single-stranded DNA primers (Ambry); (ix) chemical principle of fatty elements and water (Tilghman v. Proctor); (x) existence of cffDNA in maternal blood (Ariosa); (xi) relationship of genotype and drug response (Vanda). Examiner takeaway: identify naturally occurring principles/relations or nature-based products lacking marked differences from natural counterparts when applying the laws-of-nature/natural-phenomena exception.
